Goals Cloud computing adoption has helped small, big tech companies optimize cost, scale, and design more efficient products, but it came with its complexity. Since the infrastructure is now remote, temporary, and globally distributed, Sysadmins's control over data centers is now lost. Companies that once had a culture where Administrators and Developers had conflicting goals must change to a new culture where they now must work together as a single team aiming to build reliable software. Several new strategies and tools have emerged from observing the state of Cloud Native systems and helping such companies to keep their systems reliable in this new reality. During the design and development of an observable system, it must be instrumented to send or expose telemetry data to a third party, usually a set of tools, responsible for providing meaningful information out of the exposed data. An alternative can be autoinstrumentation, for example through the Java runtime, pprof, or eBPF. That telemetry data frequently comes in the form of metrics and logs, long used by software engineering teams, as well as traces, structured events, profiles, and crash dumps. Each signal has its purpose and best practices, and their misuse can lead to new problems when running software at scale, such as "alert fatigue" and "high cost". Even though there are several new challenges, such as culture change, capacity planning, legal issues, and others, many of them were already tackled and solved by innovative companies that entered this new era early. Beginners can learn from their findings and mistakes and follow their best practices to tackle those same issues. This paper will provide the difference between observability signals and how they should be handled, list several different methods that successful companies used when tackling common issues, present several tools that fall under the observability scope and where they should fit in your observability stack, as well as show commonly known gaps that are still unsolved or that a method still isn't very well consolidated in the market. Although this provides new strategies to build more resilient, better performant and more secure applications, it comes with the potential cost of losing control over the infrastructure supporting these workloads. Sysadmins, developers, and software operators must know the state of an application in production and the underlying infrastructure health where that application is running. Moreover, they should be able to externally observe these signals without adding, e.g. new instrumentation in the source or setting breakpoints on running production code. Applications must be designed and built to include and facilitate mechanisms that make them observable by some entity, e.g., whether this entity is another application or a human without access to the data center. The effort must be made early, beginning with design, and it often requires extra code or infrastructure automation and instrumentation. These cultural and process changes are often challenges or blockers for many organizations. On top of that, many methods and tools out in the market suggest different approaches to reach a reasonable level of observability. Once one reaches a satisfactory level of observability, there is no doubt of its benefits, but getting started can feel daunting! retrieved.title: Aggregation layer
retrieved.text:
The aggregation layer allows Kubernetes to be extended with additional APIs, beyond what is
offered by the core Kubernetes APIs.
The additional APIs can either be ready-made solutions such as a
metrics server, or APIs that you develop yourself.

The aggregation layer is different from
Custom Resource Definitions,
which are a way to make the {{}}
recognise new kinds of object.

Aggregation layer

The aggregation layer runs in-process with the kube-apiserver. Until an extension resource is
registered, the aggregation layer will do nothing. To register an API, you add an _APIService_
object, which "claims" the URL path in the Kubernetes API. At that point, the aggregation layer
will proxy anything sent to that API path (e.g.  ) to the
registered APIService.

The most common way to implement the APIService is to run an *extension API server* in Pod(s) that
run in your cluster. If you're using the extension API server to manage resources in your cluster,
the extension API server (also written as "extension-apiserver") is typically paired with one or
more {{}}. The apiserver-builder
library provides a skeleton for both extension API servers and the associated controller(s).

Response latency

Extension API servers should have low latency networking to and from the kube-apiserver.
Discovery requests are required to round-trip from the kube-apiserver in five seconds or less.

If your extension API server cannot achieve that latency requirement, consider making changes that
let you meet it.

* To get the aggregator working in your environment, configure the aggregation layer.
* Then, setup an extension api-server to work with the aggregation layer.
* Read about APIService in the API reference
* Learn about Declarative Validation Concepts,
  an internal mechanism for defining validation rules that in the future will help support validation for extension API server development.

Alternatively: learn how to extend the Kubernetes API using
Custom Resource Definitions.

retrieved.title: Enabling Peer-aggregated Discovery and Mixed Version Proxy
retrieved.text: {{}} Kubernetes {{}} includes a beta feature that lets an {{}} proxy resource requests to other _peer_ API servers. It also lets clients get a holistic view of resources served across the entire cluster through discovery. This is useful when there are multiple API servers running different versions of Kubernetes in one cluster (for example, during a long-lived rollout to a new release of Kubernetes). This enables cluster administrators to configure highly available clusters that can be upgraded more safely, by : 1. ensuring that controllers relying on discovery to show a comprehensive list of resources for important tasks always get the complete view of all resources. We call this complete cluster-wide discovery _Peer-aggregated discovery_. 1. directing resource requests (made during the upgrade) to the correct kube-apiserver. This proxying prevents users from seeing unexpected 404 Not Found errors that stem from the upgrade process. This mechanism is called the _Mixed Version Proxy_. Enabling Peer-aggregated Discovery and Mixed Version Proxy Ensure that feature gate is enabled when you start the {{}}: Proxy transport and authentication between API servers {#transport-and-authn} * The source kube-apiserver reuses the existing APIserver client authentication flags and to present its identity that will be verified by its peer (the destination kube-apiserver). The destination API server verifies that peer connection based on the configuration you specify using the command line argument. * To authenticate the destination server's serving certs, you must configure a certificate authority bundle by specifying the command line argument to the **source** API server. Configuration for peer API server connectivity To set the network location of a kube-apiserver that peers will use to proxy requests, use the and command line arguments to kube-apiserver or specify these fields in the API server configuration file. If these flags are unspecified, peers will use the value from either or command line argument to the kube-apiserver. If those too, are unset, the host's default interface is used. Peer-aggregated discovery When you enable the feature, discovery requests are automatically enabled to serve a comprehensive discovery document (listing all resources served by any apiserver in the cluster) by default. If you would like to request a non peer-aggregated discovery document, you can indicate so by adding the following Accept header to the discovery request: {{}} Peer-aggregated discovery is only supported for Aggregated Discovery requests to the endpoint and not for Unaggregated (Legacy) Discovery requests. {{}} Mixed version proxying When you enable

retrieved.title: Disabling DeclarativeValidationBeta {#opt-out}
retrieved.text: {{}} Kubernetes {{}} includes optional _declarative validation_ for APIs. When enabled, the Kubernetes API server can use this mechanism rather than the legacy approach that relies on hand-written Go code ( files) to ensure that requests against the API are valid. Kubernetes developers, and people extending the Kubernetes API, can define validation rules directly alongside the API type definitions ( files). Code authors define special comment tags (e.g., ). A code generator ( ) then uses these tags to produce optimized Go code for API validation. While primarily a feature impacting Kubernetes contributors and potentially developers of extension API servers, cluster administrators should understand its behavior, especially during its rollout phases. Declarative validation tags can apply directly to net-new API fields without requiring any lifecycle mechanism (for example, it is possible to use ). For migrating existing hand-written validations where the declarative validation is shadowing the existing hand-written validation logic, the rollout is controlled by the validation lifecycle tags ( and ) alongside the feature gate: * : (GA in v1.36, Default: , LockToDefault: ) The API server runs *both* the new declarative validation and the old hand-written validation for migrated types/fields in "shadow mode" (Alpha). The results are compared internally. * : (Beta, Default: ) Introduced in v1.36. This gate controls the enforcement of beta-stage validation rules. When enabled, rules marked as are authoritative; when disabled, they revert to shadow mode. * : (Deprecated in v1.36). Previously used to determine whether declarative validation results were authoritative. It is no longer honored but can still be set to prevent "gate not recognized" errors. **Default Behavior (Kubernetes {{}}):** * With (the default), both validation systems run for Alpha and shadowed rules. Beta rules are enforced. * **The results of the *hand-written* validation are used for Alpha rules.** The declarative validation runs in a mismatch mode for comparison. * Mismatches between the two validation systems are logged by the API server and increment the metric. This data allows contributors to identify and resolve discrepancies during the shadow phase. Administrators can explicitly disable the feature gate to force validation rules back into shadow mode if unexpected validation behavior or regressions are observed. Disabling DeclarativeValidationBeta {#opt-out} As a cluster administrator, you might consider toggling = under specific circumstances: * **Unexpected Validation Behavior:** If enabling leads to unexpected validation errors or allows objects that were previously invalid. * **Performance Regressions:** If monitoring indicates significant latency

retrieved.text: a Deployment’s rolling upgrade; databases and other stateful applications often require very specific steps in sequence to safely perform upgrades. The operator can handle this autonomously as it knows your current and requested versions and can run specialized upgrade code when needed. More generally, this can apply to anything a pre-cloud-native environment would use manual checklists for (effectively using the operator as an executable runbook). Another common way to take advantage of automated domain knowledge is error remediation. For example, the Kubernetes built-in remediation behaviours mostly start and end with “restart container until it works” which is a powerful solution but often not the best or fastest solution. 6 An operator can monitor its application and react to errors with specific behaviour to resolve the error or escalate the issue if it can’t be automatically resolved. This can reduce MTTR (mean time to recovery) and also reduce operator fatigue from recurring issues. Operator Components in Kubernetes “An operator is a Kubernetes controller that understands 2 domains: Kubernetes and something else. By combining knowledge of both domains, it can automate tasks that usually require a human operator that understands both domains” (Jimmy Zelinskie, https://github.com/ kubeflow/tf-operator/issues/300#issuecomment-357527937) Operator Big Picture Operators enable the extension of the Kubernetes API with operational knowledge. This is achieved by combining Kubernetes controllers and watched objects that describe the desired state. The controller can watch one or more objects and the objects can be either Kubernetes primitives such as Deployments, Services or things that reside outside of the cluster such as Virtual Machines or Databases. The desired state refers hereby to any resource that is defined in code and which the operator is configured to manage. Subsequently, the current state references the deployed instance of those resources. The controller will constantly compare the desired state with the current state using the reconciliation loop which ensures that the watched objects get transitioned to the desired state in a defined way. The desired state is encapsulated in one or more Kubernetes custom resources and the controller contains the operational knowledge which is needed to get the objects (such as deployments, services) to their target state. 7 Kubernetes Controllers A Kubernetes Controller takes care of routine tasks to ensure the desired state expressed by a particular resource type matches the current state (current state, https://engineering.bitnami. com/articles/a-deep-dive-into-kubernetes-controllers.html, https://fntlnz.wtf/post/what-i-learnt- about-kubernetes-controller/). In comparison, an operator can define new custom object types (custom resources) to better express the configuration of a particular application in a Kubernetes context. The aggregation layer allows Kubernetes to be extended with additional APIs, beyond what is
offered by the core Kubernetes APIs.
The additional APIs can either be ready-made solutions such as a
metrics server, or APIs that you develop yourself.

The aggregation layer is different from
Custom Resource Definitions,
which are a way to make the {{}}
recognise new kinds of object.

Aggregation layer

The aggregation layer runs in-process with the kube-apiserver. Until an extension resource is
registered, the aggregation layer will do nothing. To register an API, you add an _APIService_
object, which "claims" the URL path in the Kubernetes API. At that point, the aggregation layer
will proxy anything sent to that API path (e.g.  ) to the
registered APIService.

The most common way to implement the APIService is to run an *extension API server* in Pod(s) that
run in your cluster. If you're using the extension API server to manage resources in your cluster,
the extension API server (also written as "extension-apiserver") is typically paired with one or
more {{}}. The apiserver-builder
library provides a skeleton for both extension API servers and the associated controller(s).

Response latency

Extension API servers should have low latency networking to and from the kube-apiserver.
Discovery requests are required to round-trip from the kube-apiserver in five seconds or less.

If your extension API server cannot achieve that latency requirement, consider making changes that
let you meet it.

* To get the aggregator working in your environment, configure the aggregation layer.
* Then, setup an extension api-server to work with the aggregation layer.
* Read about APIService in the API reference
* Learn about Declarative Validation Concepts,
  an internal mechanism for defining validation rules that in the future will help support validation for extension API server development.

Alternatively: learn how to extend the Kubernetes API using
Custom Resource Definitions.

The desired state refers hereby to any resource that is defined in code and which the operator is configured to manage. query: What combined approach should an organization adopt to (1) ensure the integrity of source code and developer access, and (2) provide cryptographic guarantees for each stage of the build pipeline, and which specific practices or tools are recommended for each part?
answer:
**Combined “Secure‑Supply‑Chain” approach** | Goal | What the organization must do | Recommended practices / tools (with source) | |------|------------------------------|---------------------------------------------| | **1. Keep the source‑code repository trustworthy and limit who can touch it** | • Treat the repository as the “single source of truth”.
• Make every change verifiable and non‑repudiable.
• Enforce strict identity‑and‑access controls for both humans and automation agents. | • **Signed commits and tags** (GPG/SSH) – the white‑paper states that “Signing source code (commits and tags) ensures integrity and non‑repudiation” and is a required verification step【pdf_whitepaper†1】.
• **Protected namespaces / branch protection** – declare a protected repository namespace (e.g., *main* or *release* branches) and require review/approval before any change can be merged【pdf_whitepaper†2】.
• **IAM with least‑privilege and MFA** – “Identity and Access Management (IAM) is the biggest attack vector… policies must be calibrated to roles and require multi‑factor authentication”【pdf_whitepaper†2】.
• **Encryption‑at‑rest for secrets** – Kubernetes best‑practice guide recommends configuring encryption for Secret objects and using external secret stores (e.g., Secrets Store CSI driver)【markdown_doc†2】.
• **RBAC / role‑based access** – limit human and service‑account permissions to only what is needed (e.g., “Restrict access to Secrets to the most privileged, system‑level components”【markdown_doc†2】.
• **Audit logs & short‑lived credentials** – monitor read/write events on the repo and rotate credentials frequently (implied by the “audit rules” recommendation in the secrets guide). | | **2. Give every build‑pipeline stage a cryptographic proof that it ran correctly** | • Capture a hash of every input and output of each step.
• Sign that metadata so it can be verified later.
• Enforce the signed metadata against a policy before the next step or before deployment. | • **in‑toto layout & signed “links”** – the white‑paper describes using in‑toto to “hash and sign the inputs and output of the steps in the pipeline” and then verify them with a layout‑based workflow【pdf_whitepaper†4】.
• **Open Policy Agent (OPA)** – “Build metadata should be evaluated against the policy template by using tools such as Open Policy Agent”【pdf_whitepaper†4】.
• **SLSA (Supply‑Chain Levels for Software Artifacts)** – aim for higher SLSA levels; they require reproducible builds, signed attestations and provenance metadata【pdf_whitepaper†3】.
• **Reproducible builds** – “Ensure that binaries are consistently generated from their source code to make tampering evident”【pdf_whitepaper†3】.
• **Signed attestations / SBOM** – generate a Software Bill of Materials and a signed attestation (e.g., using cosign, Notary, or in‑toto) so downstream consumers can verify provenance【pdf_whitepaper†3】.
• **VEX (Vulnerability Exploitability Exchange)** – attach VEX data to the attestation to convey exploitability status【pdf_whitepaper†3】.
• **CI/CD isolation & minimal build environments** – run each step in a container‑isolated worker, keep the image minimal, and protect the worker’s keys in an HSM or credential manager (recommended in the “Build Pipeline” section of the cloud‑native security white‑paper)【pdf_whitepaper†5】.
• **Image scanning & policy enforcement** – integrate vulnerability scanners in CI and gate the pipeline with OPA or similar policy engines before promotion【pdf_whitepaper†5】. | ### How the two parts fit together 1. **Start with a hardened source‑code ecosystem** – signed commits, protected branches, MFA‑protected IAM, encrypted secrets, and strict RBAC give confidence that the code entering the pipeline has not been altered and that only authorized developers or agents can push it. 2. **Pass that trusted code through a “cryptographically‑audited” pipeline** – each CI step produces a hash‑linked, signed record (in‑toto link). OPA evaluates those records against a policy layout (e.g., “only code signed by a trusted key may be built”, “all dependencies must be fetched from verified hashes”). The pipeline also produces SLSA‑level artifacts: reproducible binaries, signed attestations, SBOMs, and VEX data. 3. **Downstream verification** – when the artifact is stored in an artifact registry or deployed, the signed attestation and SBOM can be checked (cosign, Notary, in‑toto verification) to prove that every upstream step complied with the organization’s policy. By **combining strong source‑code integrity controls (signed commits, IAM, protected branches, encrypted secrets) with end‑to‑end cryptographic guarantees for the build pipeline (in‑toto, OPA, SLSA, reproducible builds, signed attestations, SBOM/VEX)**, an organization creates a supply‑chain that is both *trusted at the point of entry* and *provably secure throughout the build, test, and release process*.

Sysadmins, developers, and software operators must know the state of an application in production and the underlying infrastructure health where that application is running. Moreover, they should be able to externally observe these signals without adding, e.g. new instrumentation in the source or setting breakpoints on running production code. Applications must be designed and built to include and facilitate mechanisms that make them observable by some entity, e.g., whether this entity is another application or a human without access to the data center. The effort must be made early, beginning with design, and it often requires extra code or infrastructure automation and instrumentation. These cultural and process changes are often challenges or blockers for many organizations. On top of that, many methods and tools out in the market suggest different approaches to reach a reasonable level of observability. Once one reaches a satisfactory level of observability, there is no doubt of its benefits, but getting started can feel daunting! Cultural changes, different tools, different objectives, different methods. So many details that need to be considered can make this journey confusing and painful. This paper aims to provide clarity so that more software and operations teams can gain the benefits of observability in their systems. Use these guidelines to improve the security of your sensitive information in Secret objects, as well as to more effectively manage your Secrets. Cluster administrators This section provides good practices that cluster administrators can use to improve the security of confidential information in the cluster. Configure encryption at rest By default, Secret objects are stored unencrypted in {{}}. You should configure encryption of your Secret data in . For instructions, refer to Encrypt Secret Data at Rest. Configure least-privilege access to Secrets {#least-privilege-secrets} When planning your access control mechanism, such as Kubernetes {{}} (RBAC), consider the following guidelines for access to objects. You should also follow the other guidelines in RBAC good practices. - **Components**: Restrict or access to only the most privileged, system-level components. Only grant access for Secrets if the component's normal behavior requires it. - **Humans**: Restrict , , or access to Secrets. Only allow cluster administrators to access . This includes read-only access. For more complex access control, such as restricting access to Secrets with specific annotations, consider using third-party authorization mechanisms. {{}} Granting access to Secrets implicitly lets the subject fetch the contents of the Secrets. {{}} A user who can create a Pod that uses a Secret can also see the value of that Secret. Even if cluster policies do not allow a user to read the Secret directly, the same user could have access to run a Pod that then exposes the Secret. You can detect or limit the impact caused by Secret data being exposed, either intentionally or unintentionally, by a user with this access. Some recommendations include: * Use short-lived Secrets * Implement audit rules that alert on specific events, such as concurrent reading of multiple Secrets by a single user Restrict Access for Secrets Use separate namespaces to isolate access to mounted secrets. Improve etcd management policies Consider wiping or shredding the durable storage used by once it is no longer in use. If there are multiple instances, configure encrypted SSL/TLS communication between the instances to protect the Secret data in transit. Goals Cloud computing adoption has helped small, big tech companies optimize cost, scale, and design more efficient products, but it came with its complexity. Since the infrastructure is now remote, temporary, and globally distributed, Sysadmins's control over data centers is now lost. Companies that once had a culture where Administrators and Developers had conflicting goals must change to a new culture where they now must work together as a single team aiming to build reliable software. Several new strategies and tools have emerged from observing the state of Cloud Native systems and helping such companies to keep their systems reliable in this new reality. During the design and development of an observable system, it must be instrumented to send or expose telemetry data to a third party, usually a set of tools, responsible for providing meaningful information out of the exposed data. An alternative can be autoinstrumentation, for example through the Java runtime, pprof, or eBPF. That telemetry data frequently comes in the form of metrics and logs, long used by software engineering teams, as well as traces, structured events, profiles, and crash dumps. Each signal has its purpose and best practices, and their misuse can lead to new problems when running software at scale, such as "alert fatigue" and "high cost". Even though there are several new challenges, such as culture change, capacity planning, legal issues, and others, many of them were already tackled and solved by innovative companies that entered this new era early. Beginners can learn from their findings and mistakes and follow their best practices to tackle those same issues. This paper will provide the difference between observability signals and how they should be handled, list several different methods that successful companies used when tackling common issues, present several tools that fall under the observability scope and where they should fit in your observability stack, as well as show commonly known gaps that are still unsolved or that a method still isn't very well consolidated in the market. retrieved.text: .. _community_committer_guidelines: Committers Guidelines These are the guidelines for people with commit privileges on the repositories in the ansible and ansible-collections GitHub organizations. Committers of _ are necessarily Red Hat employees acting as members of the Ansible Core team. Committers of _ are members of the community or Ansible Engineering. Please read the guidelines before you commit. These guidelines apply to everyone. At the same time, this is NOT a process document. So just use good judgment. You have been given commit access because we trust your judgment. That said, use the trust wisely. If you abuse the trust and break components and builds, and so on, the trust level falls and you may be asked not to commit or you may lose your commit privileges. Features, high-level design, and roadmap of ansible-core As a core team member, you are an integral part of the team that develops the :ref: . Please be engaged, and push for the features and fixes that you want to see. Also keep in mind that Red Hat, as a company, will commit to certain features, fixes, APIs, and so on, for various releases. Red Hat, the company, and the Ansible team must get these changes completed and released as scheduled. Obligations to users, the community, and customers must come first. Because of these commitments, a feature you want to develop yourself may not get into a release if it affects a lot of other parts within Ansible. Any other new features and changes to high level design should go through the proposal process (TBD), to ensure the community and core team have had a chance to review the idea and approve it. The core team has sole responsibility for merging new features based on proposals to _. query: When building a distributed database that must satisfy ACID guarantees, in what ways can the security principle of compartmentalization be used to reinforce the consistency and durability properties, and why is the presence of a trusted actor important for this reinforcement?
answer:
**Compartmentalization as a security‑by‑design aid for ACID** | ACID property | How compartmentalization helps | Why a trusted actor matters | |---------------|--------------------------------|-----------------------------| | **Consistency** – “guarantees that a transaction started in the future can necessarily see the effects of all transactions committed in the past and that a transaction can only move the database from one valid state to another”【pdf_whitepaper†2】 | • By placing the *transaction coordinator*, the *data‑store replicas* and the *write‑ahead log* in separate, mutually‑isolated execution domains (different processes, containers, or physical machines), a fault or a malicious code injection in one domain cannot corrupt the state that the other domains maintain.
• If a replica is compromised, the isolated coordinator can still enforce the serialisation rules and reject divergent state, preventing the compromised node from breaking the global invariant.
• Isolation of the log‑writer from the data‑writer means that an attacker who gains control of the data path cannot directly tamper with the durability log, preserving the “all‑or‑nothing” view of a transaction. | | **Durability** – “once a transaction has been committed, it will remain committed even in the case of a system failure; the effects are recorded in non‑volatile memory”【pdf_whitepaper†1】 | • Storing the durable log (or quorum of replicas) in a compartment that is *physically* or *cryptographically* separated from the front‑end service limits the attack surface: a compromise of the front‑end cannot erase or rewrite the log because the log resides in a different trust domain.
• Replication groups can be placed in distinct failure domains (different racks, zones, or clouds). If one domain fails, the other compartments still hold the committed data, satisfying durability without relying on a single point of failure. | **Why a trusted actor is required** The white‑paper on threat modelling explains that compartmentalization “helps to contain the attacker’s capabilities from a single compromise” and that “most systems have a trusted actor … responsible for indicating who the other actors are in the system”【pdf_whitepaper†4】. * The trusted actor (e.g., a root‑of‑trust service, a certificate authority, or a privileged coordinator) is the entity that **authoritatively defines and enforces the boundaries between compartments**. It signs the metadata that identifies each compartment, validates that only the designated component can write to the durability log, and vouches for the integrity of the transaction coordinator’s decisions. * Because the trusted actor is the only party that can issue or revoke the credentials that allow a compartment to modify the shared state, any breach in a non‑trusted compartment cannot forge those credentials. Consequently, even if an attacker compromises a data‑node, they cannot falsify the durability log or bypass the consistency checks without the trusted actor’s endorsement. * The presence of this single, well‑protected authority therefore **reinforces both consistency and durability**: it guarantees that the rules governing state transitions are applied uniformly (consistency) and that the committed state is recorded by an entity that cannot be spoofed (durability). **In practice** * Deploy the transaction manager in a hardened, auditable environment (e.g., a separate VM with minimal services) that acts as the trusted actor. * Keep the write‑ahead log on storage that is only writable by the trusted actor (e.g., using mount options `nosuid,nodev,noexec` or encrypted volumes) – a pattern echoed in Kubernetes hardening discussions about “read‑only root filesystem and no‑exec writable mounts”【github_issue†1】. * Isolate each replica’s data directory and network stack so that a compromise of one replica does not give direct access to the log or coordinator. By **compartmentalizing** the critical functions of a distributed database and anchoring their interaction to a **trusted actor**, the system gains stronger guarantees that transactions remain consistent and that their effects survive failures, even in the presence of partial compromises.

retrieved.text: ## Feature: local storage request/limit From v1.7, we add the feature to allow users set local storage limit for pod’s emptyDir and container’s writable layer (overlay) to better provide storage capacity isolation. For all type of resources in Kubernetes, user can set value for request and/or limit. The relationship between request and limit is defined as follows - A BestEffort quality of service is provided when a request and limit are not specified. - A Burstable quality of service is provided when a request is specified that is less than an optionally specified limit. - A Guaranteed quality of service is provided when a limit is specified that is equal to an optionally specified request. The quality of service has an impact on what happens if the resource is compressible or not. For incompressible resource such as memory, a BestEffort container will be able to consume as much resource as is available on the node. In addition, a BestEffort container has the greatest chance of being killed if there is an out of resource event on the node. A Burstable container will be scheduled on the node to get the amount of resource requested, but it may consume more. If there is an out of resource event on the node, containers of this type will be killed after BestEffort containers when attempting to reclaim resource. A Guaranteed container will get the amount of resource requested, but no more. In the event of a system out of resource event, it will only be killed if there are no more BestEffort or Burstable containers on the system. For Burstable container setting, one problem is that resource could be over-committed. The scheduler will tend to pack more Pods to the nodes. When disk is under pressure, the eviction manager will try to reclaim storage resource and evict pods to free up resource if reclaim is not enough. Storage is also an incompressible resource like memory. However, unlike memory, reclaim storage resource and free disk space take much longer time and incur more overhead. So the system would be much more stable if it can allocate enough resources for the workload at the first place to avoid reclaim. ## Proposal: request/limit validation One proposal is to enforce that request is always equal to limit for local storage. If you need a more permanent, highly available cluster, however, you should consider ways of extending the control plane. By design, one-machine control plane services running on a single machine are not highly available. started in the future can necessarily see the effects of all transactions committed in
the past. Also sometimes understood to be a guarantee that a transaction can only
bring the data from one valid state to another, while maintaining invariants (for
example that stock count cannot be less than zero, or that two customers with the
same id number cannot exist).
3. Isolation: guarantees that concurrent execution of transactions leaves the database
in the same state that would have been obtained if the transactions were executed
sequentially, in some order.
4. Durability: guarantees that once a transaction has been committed, it will remain
committed even in the case of a system failure (e.g., power outage or crash). This
usually means that completed transactions (or their effects) are recorded in
non-volatile memory.
12.3.2 The CAP Theorem
The CAP Theorem states that it is impossible for a distributed data store to simultaneously
provide more than two out of the following three guarantees:
1. Consistency: Every read receives the most recent write or an error
2. Availability: Every request receives a response that is not an error
3. Partition tolerance: The system continues to operate despite an arbitrary number of
messages being dropped (or delayed) by the network between nodes
In the absence of network failure both availability and consistency can be satisfied. CAP is
frequently misunderstood to mean that one has to choose to abandon one of the three
guarantees at all times. In fact, the choice is really between consistency and availability only
when a network partition or failure happens; at all other times, no trade-off has to be made.
Database systems designed with traditional ACID guarantees in mind such as RDBMS
choose consistency over availability, whereas systems designed around the BASE
philosophy, common in the NoSQL movement for example, choose availability over
consistency.
The PACELC theorem builds on CAP by stating that even in the absence of partitioning,
another trade-off between latency and consistency occurs.

Some distributed key-value stores trade off latency or scalability for linearizability and serializability consistency guarantees over the entire key-value space to reduce the risk of potential conflict updates. Some provide weaker consistency guarantees (either eventual consistency or stronger consistency within one single partition) but better latency guarantees. etcd, ZooKeeper, Consul, etc. provide distributed key-value store API for handling metadata or coordination. They only implement the data replication, but no sharding, to simplify the overall design and improve reliability. These systems provide strong consistency guarantees over the entire key space. Cassandra, HBase, etc. provide distributed key-value store API for managing massive amounts of data with low latency. They are similar since they are all Wide-Row key value stores. They implement both data replication and sharding. Strong consistency can be achieved for mutations within a row or within a partition, sometimes with limited availability. They do not provide strong consistency guarantees over mutations over different partitions through the entire key space. Spanner, CockroachDB,TiKV, YugabyteDB, FaunaDB, FoundationDB, etc., provide distributed key-value store API for managing massive amounts of data and strong consistency guarantees. They implement both the data replication and sharding features. Additionally, they implement distributed transactional protocols across multiple shards to support global transactions either through clocks (high accuracy physical clock or HLC) or through a single master (Calvin or similar protocols). The distributed transaction protocol typically introduces additional latency for cross shard transactions. For example, ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) properties and the CAP Theorem (concerning Consistency, Availability and Partition-tolerance) are both widely used terms, and many people assume that they understand what these terms mean. But considerably fewer people realise that “Consistency” means quite different things in those two contexts. For further details, Wikipedia and Irene Zhang’s musing provide good starting points. 12.3.1 ACID With the above caveats, for data storage systems, Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation and Durability are generally considered to mean: 1. Atomicity: a guarantee that each transaction across multiple data items is treated as a single "unit", which either succeeds completely, or fails completely, even in the case of various failures including machine crashes and network errors. 2. Consistency: Usually understood to mean guarantees about whether a transaction started in the future can necessarily see the effects of all transactions committed in the past. Also sometimes understood to be a guarantee that a transaction can only bring the data from one valid state to another, while maintaining invariants (for example that stock count cannot be less than zero, or that two customers with the same id number cannot exist). 3. Isolation: guarantees that concurrent execution of transactions leaves the database in the same state that would have been obtained if the transactions were executed sequentially, in some order. 4. Durability: guarantees that once a transaction has been committed, it will remain committed even in the case of a system failure (e.g., power outage or crash). This usually means that completed transactions (or their effects) are recorded in non-volatile memory. 12.3.2 The CAP Theorem The CAP Theorem states that it is impossible for a distributed data store to simultaneously provide more than two out of the following three guarantees: 1. Consistency: Every read receives the most recent write or an error 2. Availability: Every request receives a response that is not an error 3. An example of this is when the of the Ready condition remains or for longer than the kube-controller-manager's , which defaults to 50 seconds. This will cause either an taint, for an status, or a taint, for a status, to be added to the Node. These taints affect pending pods as the scheduler takes the Node's taints into consideration when assigning a pod to a Node. Existing pods scheduled to the node may be evicted due to the application of taints. Pods may also have {{}} that let them schedule to and continue running on a Node even though it has a specific taint. See Taint Based Evictions and Taint Nodes by Condition for more details. Capacity and Allocatable {#capacity} Describes the resources available on the node: CPU, memory, and the maximum number of pods that can be scheduled onto the node. The fields in the capacity block indicate the total amount of resources that a Node has. The allocatable block indicates the amount of resources on a Node that is available to be consumed by normal Pods. You may read more about capacity and allocatable resources while learning how to reserve compute resources on a Node. Info Describes general information about the node, such as kernel version, Kubernetes version (kubelet and kube-proxy version), container runtime details, and which operating system the node uses. The kubelet gathers this information from the node and publishes it into the Kubernetes API. Declared features {#declaredfeatures} {{}} This field lists specific Kubernetes features that are currently enabled on the node's kubelet via feature gates. The features are reported by the kubelet as a list of strings in the field of the Node object. This field is intended for newer features under active development; features that have graduated and no longer require a feature gate are considered baseline and are not declared in this field. This reflects the enablement of Kubernetes features, not the underlying operating system or kernel capabilities of the node. See Node Declared Features for more details. Heartbeats Heartbeats, sent by Kubernetes nodes, help your cluster determine the availability of each node, and to take action when failures are detected. For nodes there are two forms of heartbeats: * updates to the of a Node * Lease objects within the {{}}.

Node Conformance Test

*Node conformance test* is a containerized test framework that provides a system
verification and functionality test for a node. The test validates whether the
node meets the minimum requirements for Kubernetes; a node that passes the test
is qualified to join a Kubernetes cluster.

Node Prerequisite

To run node conformance test, a node must satisfy the same prerequisites as a
standard Kubernetes node. At a minimum, the node should have the following
daemons installed:

* CRI-compatible container runtimes such as Docker, containerd and CRI-O
* kubelet

Running Node Conformance Test

To run the node conformance test, perform the following steps:

1. Work out the value of the   option for the kubelet; for example:

    use   as the URL of the API server.
    There are some other kubelet command line parameters you may want to use:
  
   *  : If you are using  , you should
     remove the flag to run the test.

1. Run the node conformance test with command:

    

Running Node Conformance Test for Other Architectures

Kubernetes also provides node conformance test docker images for other
architectures:

|  Arch  |       Image       |
|--------|:-----------------:|
|  amd64 |  node-test-amd64  |
|  arm   |   node-test-arm   |
| arm64  |  node-test-arm64  |

Running Selected Test

To run specific tests, overwrite the environment variable   with the
regular expression of tests you want to run.

 

To skip specific tests, overwrite the environment variable   with the
regular expression of tests you want to skip.

 

Node conformance test is a containerized version of
node e2e test.
By default, it runs all conformance tests.

Theoretically, you can run any node e2e test if you configure the container and
mount required volumes properly. But **it is strongly recommended to only run conformance
test**, because it requires much more complex configuration to run non-conformance test.

Caveats

* The test leaves some docker images on the node, including the node conformance
  test image and images of containers used in the functionality
  test.
* The test leaves dead containers on the node. These containers are created
  during the functionality test.

retrieved.title: Impact of a kubelet restart
retrieved.text: System components on a node sometimes restart, either because of an upgrade, a crash, or an explicit operator action. This page describes what happens to Pods and to the node when the {{}}, the {{}}, or the node as a whole restarts. In a healthy cluster these restarts are usually safe and do not break running workloads. The sections below describe the effects to be aware of, which become more pronounced on large or heavily loaded nodes. The most disruptive case is a node reboot, which encompasses both a container runtime restart and a kubelet restart, but with more consequences because every container on the node stops first. Impact of a kubelet restart If only the kubelet restarts, the containers that are already running **continue to run**. The kubelet re-establishes its view of the Node, and reconciles the running containers against the desired state. During this period of time, the following happens: * The kubelet re-initializes and re-synchronizes its caches, which produces a burst of requests to the {{}}. On large nodes with many Pods this burst can be significant. * The node is temporarily reported as until the kubelet finishes initializing. While the node is , the {{}} does not place new Pods on it. * Node heartbeats pause while the kubelet is down and resume once it has restarted and finished initializing, when the kubelet renews its object and posts node status again. * The kubelet preserves the readiness of running containers across a restart. Each Pod's readiness drives {{}}, Endpoints, and downstream configuration (such as Gateways or Ingresses); this means that resetting container readiness on every restart would place a large load on the API server and on components that watch endpoint state, and could briefly remove healthy Pods from Service load balancing. This behavior is described in KEP-4781: Fix inconsistent container ready state after kubelet restart. Resetting container readiness to on every restart was the default behavior for a long time. The feature gate lets you revert to that behavior, but it is a deprecated legacy escape hatch that is slated for removal, so you should not rely on it. For more detail, see Pod behavior during kubelet restarts. * During the initial kubelet startup, {{}} of unused images and containers, and Pod evictions driven by node-pressure, are paused. This pause continues for a short grace period after the kubelet has completed its main startup routines.

The foundational idea of HA is that the Mean Time to Repair (MTTR), a failure must be much shorter than the Mean Time Between Failures (MTBF) (MTTR << MTBF), allowing something or someone to repair the broken component before another components breaks (two broken components would imply a degraded system for HA-1). query: In the context of containerized software development, how do practices such as maintaining a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) and propagating build‑stage metadata in multistage Docker builds help address the broader concerns that a security assessment targets, as opposed to the more bug‑focused findings of a security audit?
answer:
**Why an SBOM and build‑stage metadata matter for a security assessment** A security **assessment** (sometimes called a supply‑chain or risk assessment) is interested in the *whole* lifecycle of a container image – what code and third‑party components are inside it, where they came from, whether the build process was trusted, and whether the image can be proved to be the same one that was built. A security **audit**, on the other hand, tends to look for *bugs* in the code that is already running (e.g., insecure defaults, missing patches, mis‑configured permissions). The two practices that the CNCF white‑papers recommend directly address the broader, assessment‑level concerns: | Practice | What the white‑papers say | How it helps a security assessment | |----------|---------------------------|------------------------------------| | **Maintain a Software Bill of Materials (SBOM)** | *“Generate and distribute SBOMs to provide transparency about the versions and components in your software.”* (Software Supply Chain Best Practices v2)
*“SBOMs are a critical first step towards discovering what software components you have so then you may correlate them with known vulnerabilities.”* (Cloud‑Native Security v2) | • Gives an exhaustive inventory of every library, runtime, compiler, and OS package that ended up in the final image.
• Enables automated matching of those components against vulnerability feeds, licensing databases, or compliance rules.
• Provides a verifiable record that can be compared with the SBOM that was generated at build time; any mismatch signals a possible tampering or “ghost” component.
• Supplies the evidence that assessors need to answer questions such as “What third‑party code is shipped?” and “Can we prove the image has not been altered after build?” | | **Propagate build‑stage metadata in multistage Docker builds** | *“Metadata should be propagated across build stages so as to be available in the deployed container’s label. In this way, even if the intermediate build stages are thrown away, information about the build pipeline will persist.”* (Software Supply Chain Best Practices v1)
*“Attestations should include the CI step’s process, environment, materials, and products… Operators may use post‑build SBOM generators from binaries or images to validate the accuracy of the build‑time SBOM.”* (Cloud‑Native Security v2) | • Guarantees that the provenance (which base image was used, which build tools, which commit SHA, etc.) travels with the final image as labels or signed attestations.
• Allows an assessor to reconstruct the exact build chain without needing the intermediate images that were discarded for size reasons.
• Makes it possible to verify that *trusted* build images were used (e.g., hardened build workers) and that no un‑approved steps were inserted – a key supply‑chain risk.
• Supports “zero‑trust” policies where downstream systems automatically reject images that lack the required provenance metadata. | | **Combine both** | The white‑papers stress that *“SBOMs should be generated at build‑time and signed; the CI/CD system should sign both application and container images with signatures reproduced in the SBOM.”* (Cloud‑Native Security v2) | • When the SBOM and the propagated metadata are cryptographically signed, an assessor can verify integrity end‑to‑end: source → build → image → runtime.
• This moves the focus from “are there bugs in the code?” to “can we trust the entire supply chain and prove that it has not been compromised?” – exactly the broader set of questions a security assessment asks. | ### Bottom line - **SBOMs** give a *complete component inventory* and a basis for vulnerability, license, and compliance checks. - **Build‑stage metadata propagation** preserves *provenance* (who built it, with what tools, from which sources) even after the intermediate stages are discarded. Together they let a security assessor answer high‑level supply‑chain questions—*what is in the image, where did it come from, and can we prove it has not been tampered with*—whereas a traditional security audit would mainly surface code‑level bugs. The CNCF documents explicitly recommend both practices as part of a “secure CI/CD” and “software supply‑chain” strategy, showing that they are intended to satisfy the broader risk‑management goals of a security assessment.

Goals Cloud computing adoption has helped small, big tech companies optimize cost, scale, and design more efficient products, but it came with its complexity. Since the infrastructure is now remote, temporary, and globally distributed, Sysadmins's control over data centers is now lost. Companies that once had a culture where Administrators and Developers had conflicting goals must change to a new culture where they now must work together as a single team aiming to build reliable software. Several new strategies and tools have emerged from observing the state of Cloud Native systems and helping such companies to keep their systems reliable in this new reality. During the design and development of an observable system, it must be instrumented to send or expose telemetry data to a third party, usually a set of tools, responsible for providing meaningful information out of the exposed data. An alternative can be autoinstrumentation, for example through the Java runtime, pprof, or eBPF. That telemetry data frequently comes in the form of metrics and logs, long used by software engineering teams, as well as traces, structured events, profiles, and crash dumps. Each signal has its purpose and best practices, and their misuse can lead to new problems when running software at scale, such as "alert fatigue" and "high cost". Even though there are several new challenges, such as culture change, capacity planning, legal issues, and others, many of them were already tackled and solved by innovative companies that entered this new era early. Beginners can learn from their findings and mistakes and follow their best practices to tackle those same issues. If you don't specify a registry hostname, Kubernetes assumes that you mean the Docker public registry. You can change this behavior by setting a default image registry in the container runtime configuration. After the image name part you can add a _tag_ or _digest_ (in the same way you would when using with commands like or ). Tags let you identify different versions of the same series of images. Digests are a unique identifier for a specific version of an image. Digests are hashes of the image's content, and are immutable. Tags can be moved to point to different images, but digests are fixed. Image tags consist of lowercase and uppercase letters, digits, underscores ( ), periods ( ), and dashes ( ). A tag can be up to 128 characters long, and must conform to the following regex pattern: . You can read more about it and find the validation regex in the OCI Distribution Specification. The following is a non-exhaustive sample list of activities and deliverables that are in-scope for this TAG - Summary and overview of projects available in the community. - Catalog of reference architectures that draw from CNCF projects, combining them in useful and novel ways. - Definitions of implementations and patterns for best practices for delivering observability tooling at enterprise scale. - Tooling composition and toolchain creation based on existing projects. - Best practices for operations and monitoring workflows using CNCF Projects. - Organizing and helping to provide visibility to Meetups, Blogs, and Podcasts related to the scope of the TAG. - Guidance for application development and architecture that is observable. - Replicatable reference architectures. - Patterns for observing application delivery pipelines. -

Goals Cloud computing adoption has helped small, big tech companies optimize cost, scale, and design more efficient products, but it came with its complexity. Since the infrastructure is now remote, temporary, and globally distributed, Sysadmins's control over data centers is now lost. Companies that once had a culture where Administrators and Developers had conflicting goals must change to a new culture where they now must work together as a single team aiming to build reliable software. Several new strategies and tools have emerged from observing the state of Cloud Native systems and helping such companies to keep their systems reliable in this new reality. During the design and development of an observable system, it must be instrumented to send or expose telemetry data to a third party, usually a set of tools, responsible for providing meaningful information out of the exposed data. An alternative can be autoinstrumentation, for example through the Java runtime, pprof, or eBPF. That telemetry data frequently comes in the form of metrics and logs, long used by software engineering teams, as well as traces, structured events, profiles, and crash dumps. Each signal has its purpose and best practices, and their misuse can lead to new problems when running software at scale, such as "alert fatigue" and "high cost". Even though there are several new challenges, such as culture change, capacity planning, legal issues, and others, many of them were already tackled and solved by innovative companies that entered this new era early. Beginners can learn from their findings and mistakes and follow their best practices to tackle those same issues. This paper will provide the difference between observability signals and how they should be handled, list several different methods that successful companies used when tackling common issues, present several tools that fall under the observability scope and where they should fit in your observability stack, as well as show commonly known gaps that are still unsolved or that a method still isn't very well consolidated in the market. query: When a repository cleanup script removes specific vendor directories and then checks that the repository is unchanged, which git commands are used to confirm there are no pending changes, and how does this kind of verification highlight the mismatch observed in a Kubernetes conformance test that rejects an ES384‑signed token even though the production code permits it?
answer:
**What the repository‑cleanup script does**

The excerpts that show the typical “clean‑up‑and‑verify” sequence used by the Kubernetes publishing bot (see the GitHub‑issue logs) run a handful of Git commands that put the checkout into a known‑good state and then make sure nothing has changed:

| Step | Git command (as shown in the logs) | What it does |
|------|-----------------------------------|--------------|
| 1 | `git reset -q --hard` | Discards any local modifications and resets the index and working tree to the current `HEAD`. |
| 2 | `git clean -q -f -f -d` | Removes all untracked files and directories (the “vendor” directories that the script has just deleted). |
| 3 | `git rev-parse HEAD` (often stored in a variable) | Captures the current commit hash before the cleanup. |
| 4 | After the deletions, the script can re‑run `git rev-parse HEAD` (or `git diff --quiet`) and compare it with the saved hash. If the two hashes are identical, the repository is unchanged. The logs also show a check like `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` to confirm the current branch. |

These commands together guarantee that the working tree is clean: any stray changes would cause the hash comparison (or a `git diff --quiet` that would exit with a non‑zero status) to fail, and the script would abort.

**Why this matters for the ES384‑signed‑token conformance failure**

The same “no‑pending‑changes” verification pattern is useful for catching mismatches between what the source code *actually* does and what a test expects. In the Kubernetes conformance suite a test rejects an ES384‑signed service‑account token, even though the production code path (the `ValidateToken` implementation) allows it. If a repository‑cleanup script (or any CI step) first runs the clean‑up commands above and then **verifies that the source tree is exactly the same as the committed version**, any accidental edit—such as a stray change that disables the ES384 check—would be detected immediately because the hash comparison would differ.

Thus, the git‑based verification (`git reset --hard`, `git clean -fd`, and a hash or diff check) highlights the root cause of the conformance mismatch: the test is exercising a version of the code that **does not match** the committed source (or the test expectations). By ensuring the repository is unchanged before building and running the conformance tests, developers can quickly see that the observed behavior (token rejection) is not due to an unintended local modification, but rather a genuine discrepancy between the test’s expectations and the production logic. 

**What the knowledge base does not contain**

The excerpts do not include the exact line that runs `git diff --quiet` (or an equivalent hash comparison) after the vendor‑directory removal, nor do they contain the detailed description of the ES384‑signed‑token conformance test failure. The answer therefore relies on the general pattern of Git commands shown in the publishing‑bot logs and on the conceptual link between repository‑state verification and detecting mismatches in test outcomes.

Note that maintainers have privileged access to the repository to perform special functions such as branching for new versions and preparing Ansible documentation for publishing. If you're interested in becoming a maintainer, or want to get in touch with us, please join us on Matrix at #docs:ansible.im. We have weekly meetings on Matrix every Tuesday. See the Ansible calendar for meeting details. Requesting review from legal Any modifications to the or file must be reviewed and approved by the Red Hat open-source legal team. Send an email with the request to with on copy. Reviewing and merging dependency refreshes At the start of each week the workflows run. These workflows bump dependencies and create pull requests such as PR 2842. PRs to bump dependencies should be merged in a timely fashion. The documentation repo categorizes dependencies into separate requirements files. The weekly schedule for workflow runs also ensures fewer dependencies are bumped at a time. This granularity and isolation helps us detect incompatibilities and issues that a new version of a dependency might introduce. When reviewing PRs to refresh dependencies, look at the files changed and note the name of the requirements file. This corresponds to a check in CI; for example contains the dependencies for the check. In general, CI check will emit errors or warnings if the dependency refresh introduces an issue of some kind. So basically, during review, expand the CI checks and look for problems in the output of the relevant steps. If there are no errors, warnings or other messages and the step has run successfully, the dependency bump should be fine to approve and merge. In most cases, when a dependency refresh causes an issue, you probably need to adjust something in the appropriate session in . For example, PR 1172 bumped the version of which resulted in a warning because the session included a deprecated command. To fix the issue, PR 1191 updated the command and was merged before PR 1172. This is useful when refactoring sections of content, moving pages around, or renaming files or page headers. How the tool works scans links in the generated HTML files of the kubernetes website repository. It runs using a command which does the following: - Builds the site and generates output HTML in the directory of your local repository - Pulls the Docker image - Mounts your local repository to the Docker image - Scans the files generated in the directory and provides command line output when it encounters broken internal links What it does and doesn't check The link checker scans generated HTML files, not raw Markdown. The htmltest tool depends on a configuration file, , to determine which content to examine. The link checker scans the following: - All content generated from Markdown in directory, excluding: - Generated API references, for example https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.18/ - All internal links, excluding: - Empty hashes ( or ) and empty hrefs ( or ) - Internal links to images and other media files The link checker does not scan the following: - Links included in the top and side nav bars, footer links, or links in a page's section, such as links to CSS stylesheets, scripts, and meta information - Top level pages and their children, for example: , , - Blog posts - API Reference documentation, for example https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/generated/kubernetes-api/v1.18/ - Localizations Prerequisites and installation You must install * Docker * make Running the link checker To run the link checker: 1. Identifying and removing an unmaintained collection that has not been deprecated by its maintainers Conditions for removal A collection is considered unmaintained if multiple of the following conditions are satisfied: #. There has been no maintainer's activity in the collection repository for several months (for example, pull request merges and releases). #. CI has stopped passing (or even has not been running) for several months. #. Bug reports and bugfix PRs start piling up without being reviewed. There is no complete formal definition of an unmaintained collection. Process #. The appearance that the collection is no longer maintained and might be removed from the Ansible package has to be announced both in The Bullhorn and in the collection's issue tracker. #. At least four weeks after the notice appeared in The Bullhorn and the collection's issue tracker, the Ansible Community Engineering Steering Committee (SC) must look at the collection and vote that it considers it unmaintained. The vote must be open for at least one week. #. If the SC does not vote that the collection seems to be unmaintained, the process is stopped. The issue needs to be updated accordingly. #. If X.0.0 will be released next, set Y=X+1. If X.0.0 has already been released, but (X+1).0.0 has not yet been released, set Y=X+2. #. _. #. _. Canceling removal of an unmaintained collection Conditions #. Ansible Y has not yet been released. #. One or multiple maintainers step up, or return, to clean up the collection's state. #. There have been concrete results made by new maintainers (for example, CI has been fixed, the collection has been released, pull request authors have got meaningful feedback). Process #. The Steering Committee votes on whether the result is acceptable. #. A negative vote must come with a good explanation why the clean up work has not been sufficient. retrieved.text: tracking changes must also include a policy that indicates which parts of the repository are protected and who can make changes to them. For example, repositories typically have a primary branch such as main. Changes to this branch and a handful of others should be approved by trusted maintainers. Another example of protected namespaces are in enterprise contexts that use a monorepo to manage multiple projects. As different teams may be responsible for different projects, this should be clearly defined in the repository’s policy. Source control platforms such as GitHub and GitLab include mechanisms for specifying protected branches as well as protected files/folders. Open source tools like Peribolos (part of Prow) can be used to declare access control rules for GitHub. This tool is used by Kubernetes. Another option that also enables verification of policy enforcement is gittuf, an OpenSSF sandbox project. Authenticate and monitor repository activity The primary copy of the repository which serves as a synchronization point for all developers should limit who can push to it. query: How can an organization mitigate the performance overhead of encrypting data at rest while also ensuring that the encryption settings are deployed securely and consistently as part of an automated, least‑privilege infrastructure‑as‑code supply chain?
answer:
**Mitigating the performance cost of at‑rest encryption**

1. **Off‑load the crypto work** –  
   *Many modern storage systems and SSDs provide self‑encrypting‑drive (SED) or OPAL‑style hardware encryption.  Because the encryption is performed in the storage controller, the CPU‑bound cost that the Kubernetes API server would otherwise incur is eliminated.*  (CNCF Cloud‑Native Storage Whitepaper §4.5)【3†L1-L4】  

2. **Use accelerated crypto libraries** –  
   When encryption must be done in software, choose a provider that can take advantage of AES‑NI, GPU, or dedicated crypto‑offload cards.  The white‑paper notes that “acceleration options are available on many systems which can reduce the overhead.”【3†L1-L3】  

3. **Cache data‑encryption keys (DEKs)** –  
   An external KMS can encrypt the DEK once and the DEK can be cached in memory by the kube‑apiserver.  This avoids a round‑trip to the KMS for every write and speeds up secret creation.  (CNCF Cloud‑Native Security Whitepaper §5)【5†L1-L4】  

4. **Encrypt only what really needs it** –  
   The Kubernetes “decrypt‑data” task page explains that you can disable encryption for a particular resource type (e.g., ConfigMaps) if the performance impact is unacceptable, but you should keep it enabled for truly sensitive objects such as Secrets.  (Kubernetes docs)【1†L1-L7】  

5. **Gradual re‑encryption with StorageVersionMigration** –  
   When you change the encryption provider or rotate keys, use the built‑in StorageVersionMigration controller to rewrite objects in the background rather than pausing the cluster.  This spreads the compute cost over time.  (Kubernetes storage‑version‑migration doc)【4†L1-L8】

**Deploying the encryption configuration securely and consistently**

| Goal | How to achieve it in an IaC‑driven, least‑privilege pipeline |
|------|--------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Single source of truth** | Store the `EncryptionConfiguration` YAML in version‑controlled IaC (e.g., Helm chart, Kustomize overlay, Terraform).  The same file is applied to every control‑plane node. |
| **Automated rollout** | CI/CD jobs run `kubectl apply -f encryption‑config.yaml` (or the IaC tool’s apply command) on each control‑plane pod in a rolling fashion, respecting the “automatic reload” flag so the apiserver picks up changes without a full restart.  (Kubernetes docs)【1†L1-L5】 |
| **Least‑privilege service accounts** | Create a dedicated Kubernetes ServiceAccount that only has the `patch`/`update` permission on the `kube‑apiserver` static‑pod manifest and on the `EncryptionConfiguration` ConfigMap.  Bind it with a Role that **does not** grant any other cluster‑wide rights.  (Kubernetes RBAC best‑practice)【3†L1-L3】 |
| **Policy enforcement** | Add an admission‑controller (e.g., OPA Gatekeeper) rule that rejects any pod or API‑server manifest that does not reference the approved encryption provider as the first entry in the provider list.  This guarantees that every new cluster or node inherits the correct settings. |
| **Signed artefacts & drift detection** | Sign the IaC repository tags and have the pipeline verify the signature before applying.  Use a tool such as `kube‑audit` or `conftest` in the CI step to compare the live configuration against the committed file, failing the build on drift. |
| **Auditable key‑rotation** | Store the KMS key identifiers in a secret‑manager (e.g., HashiCorp Vault) that the pipeline can read with a short‑lived token.  Rotate the key by updating the `EncryptionConfiguration` and then trigger a StorageVersionMigration; the pipeline records the rotation event in the audit log. |
| **Testing the performance impact** | Include a post‑submit performance test (e.g., write‑throughput of Secrets) as a blocking gate in the CI pipeline, as recommended for critical performance tests.  (GitHub issue discussion on post‑submit blockers)【2†L1-L4】 |

**Putting it together**

1. **Select a hardware‑accelerated or KMS‑backed encryption provider** and enable the `cache` option for DEKs.  
2. **Define the provider in an `EncryptionConfiguration` YAML** that is part of your IaC repo.  
3. **Grant a minimal‑privilege service account** the ability to apply that file to the apiserver static‑pod manifest; no other component can modify it.  
4. **Run the IaC pipeline** (Helm/Kustomize/Terraform) in your CI/CD system; the pipeline validates the config with OPA, signs the artefact, and rolls it out to each control‑plane node.  
5. **If you need to change keys or providers**, update the YAML, push the change, and let the pipeline trigger a `StorageVersionMigration` so existing secrets are re‑encrypted gradually, avoiding a large one‑off CPU spike.  
6. **Monitor performance** with automated tests that block the pipeline on regressions, ensuring the chosen acceleration/caching strategy actually mitigates the overhead.

By combining **hardware or accelerated crypto**, **key‑caching**, and **gradual re‑encryption**, the organization keeps the runtime cost of at‑rest encryption low.  By **managing the encryption configuration as code**, **restricting the rights of the deployment service account**, and **gate‑keeping the change with policy‑as‑code and performance tests**, the same settings are deployed **securely, consistently, and with least‑privilege guarantees** across the entire infrastructure‑as‑code supply chain.

retrieved.text: ## Feature: local storage request/limit From v1.7, we add the feature to allow users set local storage limit for pod’s emptyDir and container’s writable layer (overlay) to better provide storage capacity isolation. For all type of resources in Kubernetes, user can set value for request and/or limit. The relationship between request and limit is defined as follows - A BestEffort quality of service is provided when a request and limit are not specified. - A Burstable quality of service is provided when a request is specified that is less than an optionally specified limit. - A Guaranteed quality of service is provided when a limit is specified that is equal to an optionally specified request. The quality of service has an impact on what happens if the resource is compressible or not. For incompressible resource such as memory, a BestEffort container will be able to consume as much resource as is available on the node. In addition, a BestEffort container has the greatest chance of being killed if there is an out of resource event on the node. A Burstable container will be scheduled on the node to get the amount of resource requested, but it may consume more. If there is an out of resource event on the node, containers of this type will be killed after BestEffort containers when attempting to reclaim resource. A Guaranteed container will get the amount of resource requested, but no more. In the event of a system out of resource event, it will only be killed if there are no more BestEffort or Burstable containers on the system. For Burstable container setting, one problem is that resource could be over-committed. The scheduler will tend to pack more Pods to the nodes. When disk is under pressure, the eviction manager will try to reclaim storage resource and evict pods to free up resource if reclaim is not enough. Latency is a combination of the rotational latency of the disk, the seek time for the head to move into place to read/write the data and the electronics/bus. SATA, SAS and SCSI are transports used by the operating system to access the device through a host bus adapter (HBA). Latency per operation is measured in a number of milliseconds and throughput is generally under 250MB/sec. Magnetic media generally offers the lowest cost per GB of capacity. ● SSD (with traditional interfaces such as SATA, SAS or SCSI) - a solid state disk does not have any moving parts and stores data in non-volatile memory (typically some type of flash). This allows for much lower latency operations - typically small fractions of a millisecond and allows for tens of thousands of I/O operations per second. Throughput is usually limited only to the transport utilised and measured in hundreds of MB per second.
